children.text: Every year, car crashes claim and devastate young lives across America, ranking as one of the top killers of children. Colorado roads raise the stakes even higher, as families drive twisting mountain passes, face storms that arrive without warning, and share congested highways where split-second decisions matter.
But,
why are car and booster seats so important?

Because they provide life‑saving protection tailored to a child’s age, size, and developmental stage, significantly reducing the chance of injury in a crash. Knowing which type of seat to use, how to install it, and understanding the latest Colorado safety requirements can mean the difference between a frightening incident and a protected child. At
Dormer Harpring
, we recognize how critical this knowledge is and are committed to helping families keep their children safe on every ride.
Car Seat Overview
Car seats

are essential safety devices designed to protect young passengers in the event of a collision. Unlike standard vehicle seat belts, they are engineered to support and restrain the smaller bodies of infants and children by distributing crash forces across the strongest parts of the body. From infancy through early adolescence, children require different types of restraints tailored to their growth, physical development, and seating posture, which makes it critical to choose a seat based on more than just age.

Modern car seats fall into four categories: rear-facing infant seats, forward-facing seats with a harness, booster seats, and standard vehicle seat belts. Each is designed for a specific age, weight, and maturity level to provide appropriate protection at every stage. Selecting the right seat is only part of the equation, since proper installation and consistent use are equally important for keeping children safe during a crash.
Why Use a Car Seat?
Car seats reduce the risk of injury by up to 71% for infants and 54% for toddlers in passenger vehicles, according to the
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration
(NHTSA). These aren’t just statistics; they represent real children protected from serious harm because their car seats were properly installed and age-appropriate.

The reason car seats are so effective comes down to biology. A child’s body is fundamentally different from an adult’s, with a spine, neck, and pelvis that are still developing and far more vulnerable during a collision. Standard seat belts are designed for adult bodies, which means they don’t provide adequate protection for children. A correctly fitted car seat bridges this gap by absorbing crash forces, minimizing dangerous movement, and preventing contact with the vehicle’s interior.
Many parents ask,
“Why are car and booster seats so important?”

, especially with Colorado’s strict child passenger safety laws in place. These seats are designed to protect children from serious harm in a crash and are also required by law. If a child is not adequately restrained, drivers may face fines. In situations where an injury occurs, the legal consequences can become much more serious.
Car Seat Stages

Keeping children safe in the car starts with recognizing the four main types of car seats, each built for a particular stage of growth and development. Instead of basing decisions solely on age, caregivers need to consider whether the child fits within their current seat’s height and weight limits. The
Child Passenger Safety Technician Fact Sheet
recommends moving to the next stage only after a child completely meets the required size and maturity benchmarks.
Here’s what every caregiver should know about each stage of car seat safety:
Rear-Facing Car Seat

Rear-facing car seats are designed for infants and young toddlers and offer the highest level of protection during early development. These seats support a child’s head, neck, and spine by cradling the body and distributing crash forces more evenly in the event of a collision, which is critical because a young child’s bones and muscles are still developing and vulnerable to serious injury. Children should remain in a rear-facing seat as long as possible, only moving to the next stage once they have outgrown the manufacturer’s weight or height limits.

Colorado law requires children under age 2 who weigh less than 40 pounds to ride rear-facing in the back seat when available, but safety experts recommend keeping children rear-facing as long as the seat’s height and weight limits allow.
Forward-Facing Car Seat

Forward-facing car seats are designed for children who have outgrown the rear-facing stage, typically between the ages of 2 and 4, depending on their height and weight. These seats use a five-point harness to secure the child at the shoulders, hips, and between the legs, which helps distribute crash forces across the strongest parts of the body while keeping them properly positioned during a collision.

In Colorado, forward-facing seats are required for children under age 2 who weigh more than 40 pounds, as well as for children ages 2 to 4 who weigh more than 20 pounds. Rather than rushing to the next stage, children should remain in this forward-facing seat until they reach the upper height or weight limit allowed by the manufacturer, ensuring they continue to receive full harness protection before transitioning to a booster seat.
Booster Seat

Booster seats are intended for children who have outgrown their forward-facing harness but are not yet large enough to use a seat belt on its own. At this stage, the booster helps position the child so that the vehicle’s lap and shoulder belts fit correctly, with the lap belt resting low across the hips and the shoulder belt lying flat across the chest. This proper alignment is crucial for preventing abdominal and spinal injuries in a crash, particularly because boosters help children remain seated in a stable position, which improves the overall effectiveness of the seat belt.

A child is ready for a booster when they can sit upright without slouching and pass the five-step seat belt readiness test, which evaluates how well the seat belt fits across their body and whether the child can maintain proper posture for the entire ride without leaning, shifting, or needing reminders to stay positioned correctly.
Vehicle Seat Belt

Once a child outgrows a booster seat and passes the five-step readiness test, they can start using the vehicle’s seat belt. The test requires sitting back against the seat, knees bending at the edge, the lap belt sitting low on the hips, the shoulder belt crossing the chest and shoulder, and maintaining this position throughout the ride. Even after making this transition, children belong in the back seat until at least age 13 for better protection from airbags and front-end collisions.

For the seat belt to work properly, it needs correct positioning. The belt should never ride up on the stomach or cut across the neck or face, as this increases injury risk during a crash. Caregivers should verify proper fit regularly, particularly during growth spurts or when switching vehicles.
The Correct Way to Position Car Seats

Improper car seat installation is more common than many caregivers realize, and even small mistakes can reduce a seat’s protective ability during a crash. Choosing the right position and following correct installation techniques ensures the seat functions as intended and keeps your child safer on the road.
Choose the Safest Location

The safest place to install a car seat is in the back seat, away from active front airbags, which can cause serious or even fatal injuries to children in the event of a crash. Whenever possible, the center position of the rear seat is considered optimal because it provides the greatest protection from side-impact collisions.

However, not all vehicles allow for a secure installation in the center. In those cases, placing the car seat on either side of the back seat is perfectly acceptable, as long as the seat fits tightly and can be properly secured according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Install the Car Seat Correctly

Proper installation matters just as much as selecting the right car seat. Begin by reviewing both the car seat manual and your vehicle’s owner’s manual to learn how the seat fits your specific car. Car seats can be secured using either the LATCH system (Lower Anchors and Tethers for Children) or the vehicle’s seat belt. Both approaches are equally safe when applied correctly.

After installation, the seat shouldn’t shift more than one inch in any direction when tested at the belt path. For rear-facing seats, checking the recline angle is also critical to keep the infant’s airway open. Most car seats include a built-in level or angle indicator to help achieve this adjustment accurately.
Position Your Child in the Seat

Proper harness positioning is critical for keeping your child safely secured in their car seat during travel. For rear-facing seats, the harness straps should be positioned at or slightly below the child’s shoulders. In forward-facing seats, the straps should sit at or slightly above the shoulders to provide the correct level of restraint.

To verify the harness is tight enough, perform the pinch test by attempting to pinch the webbing at the child’s shoulder. If you can pinch any slack material between your fingers, the harness is too loose and needs to be tightened until it fits snugly against the child’s body.
Common Mistakes to Avoid with Car Seats
Even careful parents and caregivers can make serious mistakes that undermine a car seat’s protective ability. Recognizing these common errors helps you prevent them and maximize your child’s safety:
Moving to the next stage too early
Loose harness straps
Installing the seat without locking the seat belt or LATCH system
Using an expired or damaged seat
Placing the child in thick clothing that interferes with harness tightness
Taking the time to check for these issues can make all the difference in how well your child’s seat performs during a crash.
Tips for Traveling Safely with Children
Beyond proper installation and age-appropriate seating, there are additional steps you can take to ensure every trip with your child is as safe as possible:
Register your car seat to receive safety recall alerts
Visit a certified
inspection station
to have your car seat professionally checked
Conduct regular checkups of harness tightness and overall seat condition
Never leave a child unattended in a parked vehicle
Schedule breaks during long trips for rest and seat checks
Use sunshades and airflow to prevent overheating in warm weather
These proactive measures help catch potential problems early and give you confidence that your child is riding safely every time you hit the road.
Car Seat Statistics in Colorado
Child passenger safety remains a serious concern across Colorado. Understanding the question
“Why are car and booster seats so important?”
starts with recognizing how often they’re misused. According to the
Colorado Department of Transportation’s

most recent report, 78% of car seats inspected in 2023 by certified child passenger safety technicians were either used incorrectly or not installed properly. This number reflects a troubling rise in misuse, up from just under 70% in 2022, and highlights an ongoing issue with both installation and day-to-day use.
Colorado Car Seat Law
According to the
Colorado Child Passenger Safety Law
, drivers are legally responsible for properly restraining all child passengers. Failure to comply is a primary offense, meaning you can be stopped and fined solely for this issue.
Here’s what Colorado law requires:
Children under 8 must be in a federally approved child safety seat
The seat must match the child’s age, weight, and height
Installation must follow both vehicle and car seat manufacturer’s instructions
Children under 13 must ride in the back seat when available
Violations can lead to fines and potential charges if injury occurs during non-compliance.
